description: DoS, hacking, malware and social engineering — what each threat is, how it works, and the damage it causes.
hero_image_caption: A warning screen indicating a ransomware attack has encrypted files on a computer system.
content_html:
The Cyber-Security Threat Landscape

Cyber-security threats are deliberate attempts to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to IT systems or data. The spec groups threats into four categories: Denial of Service (DoS), hacking, malware and social engineering. You must be able to define each named threat, explain how it works and describe the damage it causes.

Denial of Service (DoS)

A DoS attack floods a server, network or website with so many requests that it becomes overwhelmed and unable to respond to legitimate users. Businesses lose revenue and reputation when customers cannot access their services. A distributed DoS (DDoS) attack uses many computers at once, often as part of a botnet. It is far more powerful than a single-machine attack and much harder to block.

Hacking

Hacking refers to a person gaining unauthorised access to a system. The spec distinguishes three types by motive and authorisation status. Black hat hackers act with malicious intent: stealing data, installing malware, demanding ransoms or causing disruption for financial or political gain. Grey hat hackers access systems without permission but do not intend damage — they may discover a vulnerability and inform the organisation, sometimes without asking first. White hat hackers are authorised security professionals hired to test systems for weaknesses and fix them before attackers exploit them.

The legal status matters: black and grey hat hackers both access systems without permission (illegal); white hat hackers operate with explicit written permission (legal). A grey hat hacker who reports a flaw without permission still broke the law by accessing the system, even if their intent was benign.

Key Fact

Black hat = malicious, unauthorised. Grey hat = non-malicious but still unauthorised (discloses vulnerabilities without permission). White hat = authorised security professional, paid to find and fix vulnerabilities. The difference is permission and intent, not just intent.

Malware

Malware is the umbrella term for any malicious software. The spec lists seven named types. A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file and spreads when that file is shared — it requires human action (opening a file) to spread. A worm spreads automatically across networks without any user action. A Trojan horse disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it, then performs harmful actions secretly. A ransomware attack encrypts the victim’s files and demands a payment for the decryption key. Spyware secretly monitors user activity and sends data (such as passwords or browsing history) to the attacker. Adware floods the device with unwanted adverts and may redirect browsers to malicious sites. A botnet (mentioned above) turns the infected device into a “zombie” that the attacker controls remotely — often used for DDoS attacks or sending spam.

Social engineering exploits human behaviour, not software flaws. The spec lists six methods. Phishing uses fake emails or websites that appear to come from a trusted source (a bank, a delivery company) to trick victims into entering passwords or personal details. Pretexting involves the attacker creating a convincing fake scenario (pretending to be IT support, for example) to persuade a victim to share information or grant access.

Baiting tempts victims with something attractive — for example, leaving a USB drive labelled “Payroll 2024” in a car park. A curious employee plugs it into a work computer, infecting the network. Quid pro quo offers something in exchange for information — an attacker may phone an employee claiming to be IT support and offer to fix a problem in exchange for login credentials. Scareware displays frightening fake warnings (e.g. “Your computer is infected with 15 viruses! Click here to fix it!”) to panic users into downloading malware or paying for fake security software. Shoulder surfing is the simplest method: the attacker physically observes a victim entering a PIN, password or sensitive information in a public place.

Key Fact

The six social engineering methods are: phishing, pretexting, baiting, quid pro quo, scareware and shoulder surfing. A common exam error is naming only phishing — all six are examinable and each has a distinct mechanism.

Impacts of a Cyber-Security Attack

The spec lists six categories of impact. Data destruction: files are permanently deleted or overwritten, potentially destroying years of records. Data manipulation: data is altered without authorisation, producing incorrect outputs (e.g. changing a bank balance). Data modification: closely related to manipulation — data is changed (e.g. altering a student’s exam record). Data theft in transit and at rest: data is intercepted while being transmitted (“in transit”, e.g. captured over an unencrypted Wi-Fi connection) or stolen from stored files (“at rest”, e.g. a breached database). Denial of service to authorised users: a DoS or ransomware attack stops legitimate users from accessing systems they rely on. Identity theft: personal data (name, address, payment card details) is stolen and used to impersonate the victim, opening accounts or making purchases fraudulently.

An individual may face financial loss (fraudulent transactions, ransom payments), emotional distress (privacy violation, fear of identity theft), and the considerable time and effort needed to reclaim a stolen identity. An organisation faces financial losses (ransomware payments, lost revenue during downtime, regulatory fines), reputational damage (customers lose trust and take their business elsewhere), operational disruption (staff cannot work while systems are offline) and legal liability (if customer data was not properly protected).
exam_tip_html: For the 9-mark “discuss” or “evaluate” question, the examiner is looking for a balanced, reasoned answer, not a list. If the question asks you to discuss the impact of a cyber-attack on a small business, structure your answer: describe one impact in detail (e.g. data theft leading to loss of customer trust), explain the knock-on consequences (financial loss, potential regulatory fine), then move to a second impact with the same depth. End with a justified judgement such as “the most damaging impact is … because …”. Answers that only list impacts without reasoning cap at the lower bands.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are four cyber-security threat categories: DoS (flooding a system to deny access), hacking (black/grey/white hat, distinguished by permission and intent), malware (seven named types: virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware, spyware, adware, botnet) and social engineering (six named methods: phishing, pretexting, baiting, quid pro quo, scareware, shoulder surfing).
  • The six impacts of a cyber-security attack are: data destruction, data manipulation, data modification, data theft (in transit/at rest), denial of service to authorised users and identity theft.
  • Impacts affect individuals (financial loss, emotional distress, identity theft) and organisations (financial damage, reputational harm, operational disruption, legal liability) differently — both perspectives may be tested.

practice_questions.text: Which type of malware displays fake security warnings to trick users into downloading harmful software?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Scareware (only). Distractors: ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), phishing (fake emails/websites), adware (unwanted advertisements).

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a black hat hacker and a white hat hacker.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: black hat hacker gains unauthorised access with malicious intent to steal data or cause damage (1); white hat hacker is an authorised security professional hired to find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them (1). Award 1 mark if only one type is described accurately. Accept equivalent wording — the key distinction is authorisation status and intent.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of malware that spreads automatically across a network without any user action.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: worm (only). Do not accept virus (requires human action to spread by opening an infected file) or Trojan horse (disguises itself as software; does not self-replicate across networks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a phishing attack works and describe one way an individual can protect themselves from it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): explains that a phishing attack uses a fake email or website designed to look like a trusted source (1); explains how this tricks the victim into entering sensitive information such as passwords or bank details (1); names a specific protective action with a reason, e.g. checking the sender email address carefully (because phishing emails often use addresses with slight misspellings), or hovering over links before clicking to verify the URL (1).
Secure (2): mechanism described with one protection, but link between them is weak.
Developing (1): phishing identified as a fake email without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of a ransomware attack on a small independent dental practice that stores patient records digitally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): detailed analysis of at least two distinct impacts with scenario-specific development; balanced consideration of both immediate and longer-term consequences; supported judgement on the most severe impact.
Impact 1 (e.g. data theft/encryption): ransomware encrypts all patient records — the practice cannot access appointment history, treatment plans or medical notes, so it cannot safely treat patients. This creates immediate operational shutdown, causing lost appointment revenue and potentially endangering patient safety if emergency treatment records are unavailable.
Impact 2 (e.g. financial and reputational): paying the ransom does not guarantee file recovery; regulatory fines may follow if patient data was inadequately protected under data protection legislation; patients who hear their medical data was compromised lose trust in the practice, reducing the patient list long-term.
Judgement: e.g. 'The most damaging impact is the operational shutdown, because a dental practice with no access to patient records cannot function safely, making it the most immediate and potentially life-affecting consequence.'
Secure (5–7): two impacts described with some development; judgement present but not fully justified.
Developing (3–4): two impacts named with limited development; no judgement.
Emerging (1–2): one vague impact; no scenario link.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two impacts of a cyber-security attack on an individual.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks, one per impact: financial loss — e.g. money stolen through fraudulent transactions using the individual's compromised payment details (1); identity theft — personal data stolen and used to open accounts or make purchases in the individual's name without their knowledge (1); emotional distress — anxiety or fear caused by the privacy violation and the effort needed to reclaim a stolen identity (1). Award 1 mark per distinct, described impact.

knowledge_checks.q: A grey hat hacker is best described as someone who:
options: is paid by an organisation to find and fix vulnerabilities
gains unauthorised access with malicious intent to steal data
gains unauthorised access but without malicious intent, often disclosing vulnerabilities found
creates malware to distribute via phishing emails

knowledge_checks.q: Which social engineering method involves leaving an infected USB drive in a public place to tempt victims into plugging it into a work computer?
A _____ attack encrypts the victim's files and demands a payment for the decryption key.
A _____ is a network of infected computers controlled by an attacker without their owners' knowledge, often used to carry out DDoS attacks.
Match each cyber-security impact to its description.
right: Personal data stolen and used to impersonate the victim
Data intercepted while being transmitted over a network
Legitimate users blocked from accessing a system

flashcard_questions.q: What is a Denial of Service (DoS) attack?
flashcard_questions.a: Flooding a server with requests so it cannot respond to legitimate users.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes a black hat hacker from a white hat hacker?
flashcard_questions.a: Black hat is unauthorised and malicious; white hat is authorised and hired to find flaws.
Malware disguised as legitimate software to trick users into installing it.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
flashcard_questions.a: A virus needs human action (opening a file) to spread; a worm spreads automatically.
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment for the decryption key.
Software that secretly monitors user activity and sends data to an attacker.
Fake emails or websites mimicking a trusted source to steal login or personal details.
Physically watching someone enter a PIN or password in a public place.

flashcard_questions.q: What is quid pro quo social engineering?
flashcard_questions.a: Offering a favour (e.g. IT help) in exchange for login credentials.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six impacts of a cyber-security attack.
flashcard_questions.a: Data destruction, manipulation, modification, theft (in transit/at rest), denial of service to authorised users, identity theft.

glossary_terms.definition: An attack that floods a system or network with traffic to make it unavailable to legitimate users.
A network of computers infected with malware and controlled without their owners' knowledge, used to carry out coordinated attacks such as DDoS.
Hackers who gain unauthorised access to a system with malicious intent, such as stealing data or causing damage, for personal gain or criminal purposes.
Hackers who gain unauthorised access but without malicious intent — they typically find vulnerabilities and disclose them, sometimes publicly, without permission to access the system.
Security professionals who are paid by an organisation to attempt to hack their own systems in order to find and fix vulnerabilities before malicious attackers do.
Malicious software designed to damage, disrupt, steal data from or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
Attacks that exploit human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities to trick people into revealing confidential information or taking harmful actions.
